Date: 2026-10-24 (Europe/Zurich)
CPU: Intel Core i7-11800H @ 2.30 GHz, 16 logical CPUs; AVX=true, AVX2=true
Toolchain: go1.27.3 windows/amd64, GOEXPERIMENT=simd, GOAMD64=v1, PGO off
Base commit for both builds: 4d8d4ece23bf25513173fa1932b21dab30a7e975

Go SIMD support:
  simd/archsimd supports AVX2, including X86.AVX2() runtime detection and
  BroadcastFloat64x4. The local Go 1.27.3 source marks that broadcast as AVX2.
  https://go.dev/blog/archsimd
  https://pkg.go.dev/simd/archsimd@go1.27.3#BroadcastFloat64x4

Experiment:
  avx: unchanged AVX cost scan at the base commit.
  avx2: the same scan with candidate.patch applied. If X86.AVX2() is true,
    initialize the comparison threshold with BroadcastFloat64x4; otherwise
    retain the original AVX load from four repeated scalars. The existing
    non-AVX/scalar fallback, comparisons, tail handling and VZEROUPPER remain.
  This tests one AVX2 broadcast optimization, not every possible AVX2 algorithm.
  Both paths still compare four float64 values per 256-bit vector.
  The prototype is retained as a patch; production Go sources are unchanged.

Assembly inspection:
  avx-assembly.txt shows four scalar stack stores followed by a vector load.
  avx2-assembly.txt shows the CPU feature guard and VBROADCASTSD X0, Y0 on the
  AVX2 branch. VZEROUPPER is retained before returning to scalar code.
  Captured with:
    go tool objdump -s 'github.com/ralscha/zopfli-go.firstImprovableLength$' <binary>

Build and input controls:
  Sources were extracted with git archive into two separate temporary trees.
  Both received the same temporary digest-reporting and CPU feature test files.
  Build each with GOEXPERIMENT=simd GOAMD64=v1 go test -c -pgo=off -o <binary>.
  Apply candidate.patch only to the avx2 tree.
  All benchmark binaries run from the working repository root, using the same
  CRLF fixtures and seeded random corpus as the earlier comparison. See the
  parent directory's fixture-digests.txt and input-digests.txt.
  GOFLAGS, GODEBUG and GOMAXPROCS unset for timing; -test.cpu=1 sets one Go CPU.
  No explicit CPU affinity. Benchmarks run sequentially; no concurrent tests,
  builds or other benchmark commands.

Initial end-to-end comparison (avx.txt and avx2.txt):
  <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkPureGoGzip$ -test.benchtime=2x -test.count=1 -test.cpu=1
  Six samples per build, two timed compressions per sample. Order alternates:
    rounds 1, 3, 5: avx, avx2
    rounds 2, 4, 6: avx2, avx
  run-order.txt records invocation timestamps. Each invocation also includes
  Go's untimed calibration run. Default gzip, 15 iterations, block splitting on.
  Medians are the mean of the third and fourth sorted samples; none are removed.

Initial medians (milliseconds):
Corpus             AVX       AVX2      Time saved vs AVX
tiny-text             8.80      8.04        8.6%
mixed-256k         1520.70   1472.30        3.2%
web-assets-256k     434.75    421.00        3.2%
records-logs-256k   511.04    499.85        2.2%
real-files-256k     449.00    435.52        3.0%
random-256k         123.76    120.00        3.0%
  These short samples were noisy: AVX2 mixed-256k ranged from 1448.95 to
  2543.48 ms, and AVX tiny-text from 8.16 to 14.78 ms. A separate longer run
  checks whether the small end-to-end gains persist; both runs are retained.

Longer confirmation (confirmation-avx.txt and confirmation-avx2.txt):
  <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkPureGoGzip$ -test.benchtime=5x -test.count=1 -test.cpu=1
  Reuses the same binaries, inputs and settings, after the initial timing,
  scan benchmarks, digest checks and full suites have finished.
  Six samples per build, five timed compressions per sample; order alternates:
    rounds 1, 3, 5: avx2, avx
    rounds 2, 4, 6: avx, avx2
  confirmation-order.txt records timestamps. No samples are removed.

Confirmation medians (milliseconds):
Corpus             AVX       AVX2      Time saved vs AVX
tiny-text             8.20      7.85        4.3%
mixed-256k         1478.97   1428.98        3.4%
web-assets-256k     432.98    429.54        0.8%
records-logs-256k   507.13    497.02        2.0%
real-files-256k     446.63    434.79        2.7%
random-256k         123.69    121.48        1.8%
  Saved = 100 * (1 - median AVX2 / median AVX), using unrounded medians.

Confirmation sample ranges (milliseconds):
Corpus             AVX                 AVX2
tiny-text             8.06 -    8.49       7.76 -    9.96
mixed-256k         1464.70 - 1534.43    1409.13 - 1452.01
web-assets-256k     430.01 -  446.26     416.98 -  446.37
records-logs-256k   498.67 -  566.91     487.27 -  523.55
real-files-256k     437.38 -  449.33     425.92 -  440.79
random-256k         118.86 -  129.90     118.51 -  126.97
  The extra median reduction is 0.8-4.3% on compressible inputs. All six AVX2
  mixed-256k samples are faster than all six AVX samples. The other ranges
  overlap; random data's 1.8% difference is within the observed variation.
  This is a modest incremental benefit over AVX on this computer, with a much
  larger effect on early-hit microbenchmarks below. The unchanged AVX baseline
  was remeasured alongside the prototype; do not substitute an older run's
  baseline when attributing gains to AVX2.

Focused scans (avx-scan.txt and avx2-scan.txt):
  <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkFirstImprovableLength$ -test.benchtime=200ms -test.count=1 -test.cpu=1
  Six rounds using the same alternating order as the initial compression run,
  performed after compression timing and before digest checks or full tests.
  Selected median scan times (nanoseconds):
    length-16/hit-0:     AVX 9.1555, AVX2 2.9035 (68.3% less time)
    length-16/hit-8:     AVX 9.6215, AVX2 3.8435 (60.1% less time)
    length-64/hit-32:    AVX 11.200, AVX2 7.1485 (36.2% less time)
    length-256/hit-0:    AVX 9.1320, AVX2 2.8690 (68.6% less time)
    length-256/hit-128:  AVX 31.920, AVX2 28.270 (11.4% less time)
    length-256/hit-256:  AVX 51.330, AVX2 51.210 (0.2% less time)
  The threshold setup benefits early hits; the long no-hit scan changes little.
  Length-3 cases use the scalar path in both builds and have mixed differences.

Correctness:
  avx-checks.txt and avx2-checks.txt record successful pre-benchmark boundary,
  NaN, tie, alignment and golden-output tests, plus detected CPU features.
  All benchmark invocations perform gzip round-trip checks.
  avx-digests.txt and avx2-digests.txt each contain 18 output SHA-256 digests:
  all six corpora with default and fast gzip, plus a generated fixture with
  both profiles in gzip, zlib and deflate formats. Both match the parent
  directory's saved SIMD digests, which match the other computer's results.
  Allocation bytes and counts match between builds for each corpus.
  validation.txt records full-suite passes with SIMD enabled and disabled,
  plus the attempted GODEBUG overrides described below.

Windows fallback validation correction:
  On this Go 1.27.3 Windows runtime, GODEBUG=cpu.avx2=off and
  GODEBUG=cpu.avx=off,cpu.avx2=off leave both archsimd feature probes true.
  The runtime's getGodebugEarly in GOROOT/src/runtime/proc.go excludes Windows.
  Thus the entries labelled avx-fallback and scalar-fallback in validation.txt
  do not establish fallback coverage, despite passing. The earlier computer
  comparison's GODEBUG-based fallback claim has been corrected as well.
  Explicit checks use two temporary copies of the prototype source:
    forced-avx: replace archsimd.X86.AVX2() with false.
    forced-scalar: replace !archsimd.X86.AVX() with true.
  Run GOEXPERIMENT=simd GOAMD64=v1 go test -pgo=off -count=1 ./... in each.
  These exercise the fallback algorithms; they do not emulate older hardware.
  Results are retained in forced-fallback-validation.txt.
